records.themeTitle: Rest makes room for the life of attachment to God
records.themeSummary: The tranquility called life is valuable because it lets the soul attach itself to its Creator. Bodily comfort removes obstacles, while the life it serves comes from that attachment.
records.originHebrew: [וְאֵין הַכַּוָּנָה בְּשַׁלְוָה גּוּפָנִית לְבַד וּלְהִתְעַנֵּג בַּחֲמוּדוֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, דְּזֶה וַדַּאי אֵינוֹ חַיִּים, וְלֹא דִּבְּרָה תּוֹרָה בַּמֵּתִים אוֹתָם שֶׁבְּחַיֵּיהֶם קְרוּיִם מֵתִים (בְּרָכוֹת י״ט עַמּוּד א׳), וּבְתָמִיד [ל״ב עַמּוּד א׳]: "מַה יַּעֲשֶׂה אָדָם וְיִחְיֶה? יָמִית אֶת עַצְמוֹ; מַה יַּעֲשֶׂה אָדָם וְיָמוּת? יְחַיֶּה אֶת עַצְמוֹ", וְאֵין נִקְרָא חַי אֶלָּא הַדָּבוּק בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: "וְאַתֶּם הַדְּבֵקִים וְגוֹמֵר חַיִּים כֻּלְּכֶם", וְאֵין נִקְרָא חַי אֶלָּא כְּשֶׁהַחַיּוּת דָּבוּק בּוֹ וְאֵין נִפְרָד, וְעַל כָּל אֶחָד [בְּרָכוֹת י״ח עַמּוּד ב׳]: "בֶּן אִישׁ חַי" — צַדִּיקִים שֶׁבְּמִיתָתָן קְרוּיִם חַיִּים, וְזֶהוּ נִקְרָא חַי סְתָם, דְּאֵין חַיּוּת אֶלָּא הַנִּמְשָׁךְ מֵחֵי הָעוֹלָמִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְאַתָּה מְחַיֶּה אֶת כֻּלָּם", וְזוּלַת זֶה אֵינוֹ חַיּוּת, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁהוּא יִתְבָּרַךְ קַיָּם לָעַד, כָּךְ הַחַיּוּת הַנִּמְשָׁךְ מִמֶּנּוּ; רַק כַּוָּנַת הַמְּנוּחָה וְסִלּוּק הַטְּרָדוֹת וְהַצַּעַר בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה כְּדֵי שֶׁיִּהְיֶה נַפְשׁוֹ בְּנִיחָא לִדָּבֵק בְּקוֹנָהּ, שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר כְּשֶׁיֵּשׁ דְּבָרִים הַמַּטְרִידִים הַלֵּב וּמְבַלְבְּלִים הָאָדָם, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּעֵירוּבִין (ס״ה עַמּוּד א׳): "אִי קְרָצַתַּן כִּנָּה לָא תָּנָאֵי", וְעַל זֶה הוּא צֹרֶךְ נִיחָא דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה].
records.originEnglish: [The intention is not merely bodily tranquility and delight in the desirable things of this world. That certainly is not life; the Torah was not speaking of the dead, those who are called dead while alive. Tamid says: “What should a person do to live? Mortify himself. What should a person do to die? Keep himself alive.” Only someone attached to the blessed God is called living, as it says, “You who cleave ... are all alive.” One is called living only when life remains attached to him and is not separated. Thus, on “the son of a living man,” the Sages speak of the righteous who are called living even in death. This is what is called life without qualification: there is no life except that which flows from the Life of the worlds, as it is written, “You give life to them all.” Apart from this there is no life. Just as He endures forever, so does the life that flows from Him. The intention of rest and the removal of troubles and pain in this world is that the soul should be at ease to attach itself to its Maker. This is impossible when things trouble the heart and confuse the person. As they said in Eruvin, “If a louse bit me, I did not study.” This is why ease in this world is needed.]

records.targetHebrew: כְּתִיב (יְשַׁעְיָה מד, ג): "כִּי אֶצָּק מַיִם עַל צָמֵא וְנֹזְלִים עַל יַבָּשָׁה", כַּאֲשֶׁר הִתְחִיל אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם לְבַקֵּשׁ וּלְחַפֵּשׂ אַחַר שֹׁרֶשׁ הַחַיִּים שֶׁלּוֹ, אַחֲרֵי הֲבִינוֹ אֲשֶׁר כָּל חֶמְדַּת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה לֹא יִתָּכְנוּ לְהִקָּרְאוֹת בְּשֵׁם חַיִּים אֲמִיתִּיִּים, כִּי כָּל חֶמְדַּת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה הוּא רַק לְהָסִיר טְרָדוֹת וְהַמְּנִיעוֹת; וְאַחֲרֵי אֲשֶׁר יִתְבַּטְּלוּ כָּל הַטְּרָדוֹת, מַה יִּהְיֶה גּוּף הַחַיִּים אֲשֶׁר עָלָיו נִבְרֵאת הָעוֹלָם? עַל זֶה אָמַר לוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ: "לֶךְ לְךָ" – הַיְינוּ לְעַצְמְךָ, כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת כָּל דִּבְרֵי הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לֹא יִקָּרְאוּ בְּשֵׁם חַיִּים, וְעִיקַּר הַחַיִּים תִּמְצָא בְּךָ: (יְשַׁעְיָה מא, טז) "וְאַתָּה תָּגִיל בַּה', בִּקְדוֹשׁ יִשְׂרָאֵל תִּתְהַלָּל" – זֹאת הוּא הַחַיִּים.
records.targetEnglish: It is written, “For I shall pour water upon the thirsty, and streams upon the dry ground.” When Abraham our father began to seek and search for the root of his life, he understood that all the desirable things of this world could not be called true life. All this world’s desirable things serve only to remove troubles and obstacles. Once all the troubles have been removed, what will constitute life itself, for which the world was created? Concerning this the blessed God told him, “Go for yourself”—that is, to yourself. In truth, none of the things of this world are called life. You will find the essence of life within yourself: “You shall rejoice in the Lord; in the Holy One of Israel you shall glory.” This is life.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach supplies the question that distinguishes the means from the end in Divrei Soferim. Once discomfort is removed, one must still ask what the resulting freedom is for. Abraham discovers that life consists in rejoicing in God; Divrei Soferim explains why ordinary rest remains necessary as room for that attachment. Together the passages keep tranquility from being mistaken either for the whole of life or for something without spiritual purpose.

records.reverseExplanation: Divrei Soferim explains the continuing place of ordinary ease in Abraham’s search: relief from disturbance enables attachment to the Creator, even though relief is not itself the life being sought. This gives a practical purpose to the removal of obstacles described by Mei HaShiloach.
records.reverseThemeTitle: Seeking life after the obstacles have been removed
records.reverseThemeSummary: Abraham asks what life itself consists of when worldly pleasures have removed discomfort. “Go for yourself” directs him inward toward rejoicing in God, the root of true life.

records.themeTitle: Repentance extends from stopping a sin to guarding its surroundings
records.themeSummary: Repentance can bring real release before the past has been completely repaired. Extending restraint to the conditions around a sin prevents renewed descent and gives the work of return greater strength.
records.originHebrew: אֲבָל גָּלוּת בָּבֶל הוּא גָּלוּת הָרִאשׁוֹנָה שֶׁהָיְתָה בִּשְׁבִיל הַחֵטְא, וּגְאֻלָּתוֹ הוּא גְּאֻלָּה הָרִאשׁוֹנָה שֶׁהָיְתָה עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה ״שֶׁמְּבִיאָה גְּאֻלָּה״; וְזֶה נֶגֶד מִדַּת הַנֶּצַח — הַיְינוּ נִיצּוּחַ — שֶׁכָּל גְּאֻלָּה הוּא נִיצּוּחַ הָאֻמָּה הַמְּשַׁעְבֶּדֶת, שֶׁכָּל כֹּחַ שֶׁעֲבוֹדָה לְיִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא מִצַּד הַחֵטְא שֶׁהוּא בְּפֹעַל וְעַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁמְּתַקֵּן מִכָּאן וּלְהַבָּא לְבַד, דְּנִתְבַּטֵּל מַעֲשֵׂה הַחֵטְא בְּפֹעַל אַף שֶׁלֹּא נִתְקַן הַשֹּׁרֶשׁ דִּלְמַפְרֵעַ — וַעֲדַיִין אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיַּחֲזֹר לְקִלְקוּלוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁהָיָה אָז שֶׁגָּלוּ שֵׁנִית — מִכָּל מָקוֹם מִצַּד כֹּחַ הַתְּשׁוּבָה בְּתִיקּוּן דִּלְהַבָּא , שֶׁנִּתְבָּאֵר [בְּסִימָן א] בַּהֲבָאַת רְפוּאָה, דְּהוּא גַּם כֵּן אַף שֶׁלֹּא נִתְקַן בְּהֶחְלֵט, הָכִי נָמֵי הֲבָאַת גְּאֻלָּה עַל דֶּרֶךְ זֶה כִּי אֵין השי"ת מַבִּיט בָּזֶה אֶלָּא עַל מַה שֶּׁהוּא אוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה; רַק צָרִיךְ לָזֶה תְּשׁוּבָה בְּתֹקֶף יוֹתֵר, שֶׁיּוֹעִיל לְנַצֵּחַ הָאֻמָּה שֶׁכְּבָר נִמְסְרוּ לְיָדָן בְּסִבַּת הַחֵטְא שֶׁזֶּהוּ עַל דֶּרֶךְ ״עֲבֵירָה גּוֹרֶרֶת עֲבֵירָה״ וְ״הַבָּא לְטַמֵּא פּוֹתְחִין [לוֹ]״, שֶׁהֲרֵי שִׁעְבּוּדָם גּוֹרֵם לַחֲטוֹא עוֹד יוֹתֵר וְאָמְרוּ [פְּסָחִים קיח:] דִּ״כְלוּם יֵשׁ עֶבֶד שֶׁרַבּוֹ נוֹתֵן לוֹ מַתָּנָה וְחוֹזֵר וְנוֹטְלָהּ מִמֶּנּוּ״; וְאַף דְּגָלוּת יִשְׂרָאֵל חָלִילָה לֹא הָיָה דֶּרֶךְ מַתָּנָה כְּלָל, מִכָּל מָקוֹם הֲרֵי לְפִי שָׁעָה נִגְזַר לִהְיוֹת תַּחַת יָדָם, וְצָרִיךְ עַל זֶה מִשְׁפָּט בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ שֶׁיּוּכְלוּ לְנַצְּחָם וְלָצֵאת מִתַּחַת יָדָם וְשֹׁרֶשׁ הַתְּשׁוּבָה, דְּהוּא הַחֲרָטָה מֵהַחֵטְא וּשְׁמִירָה מִמֶּנּוּ לְהַבָּא — הִנֵּה קַבָּלַת הַשְּׁמִירָה מִגּוּף הַחֵטְא עַצְמוֹ מֵבִיא רְפוּאָה לְמַכַּת הַחֵטְא, וְהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּתוֹ הוּא קַבָּלַת גְּדֵרִים וּסְיָיגִים עַל עֶצֶם הַדָּבָר שֶׁסְּבִיבוֹת הַחֵטְא, שֶׁלֹּא יָבוֹא לִידֵי חֵטְא — זֶהוּ הַגּוֹרֵם גְּאֻלָּה וְנִיצּוּחַ לָאֻמָּה הַמְשֻׁעְבֶּדֶת, בִּהְיוֹתוֹ מִתְרַחֵק עַל יְדֵי זֶה מֵהַחֵטְא לְגַמְרֵי
records.originEnglish: The Babylonian exile, however, was the first exile caused by sin, and its redemption was the first redemption through repentance, which “brings redemption.” This corresponds to the quality of netzach—that is, victory—for every redemption is a victory over the nation that enslaves, whose entire power to enslave Israel comes from sin in actual deed. Through repentance that repairs only from now onward, the sinful deed is annulled in practice even though its root has not been repaired retroactively. It remains possible that the person will return to his corruption, as happened then, when they were exiled again. Nevertheless, repentance’s power to repair the future, explained in section one concerning the bringing of healing even where the repair is not definitive, likewise brings redemption in this manner. For in this matter the blessed God looks only at what the person is at that time. Yet repentance of greater force is needed, so that it can overcome the nation into whose hands they were already delivered because of sin. This follows “one transgression draws another” and “one who comes to defile himself is given an opening,” since their subjugation causes still more sin. They said in Pesachim: “Does a master give a servant a gift and then take it back?” Although Israel’s exile was certainly not a gift, God forbid, they were nevertheless decreed for the time being to be under those nations’ power. A separate judgment is needed for them to overcome the nations and emerge from beneath their power. The root of repentance is regret for sin and guarding against it in the future. Accepting the duty to guard against the sinful act itself brings healing to the wound of sin. Its extension is accepting boundaries and safeguards concerning the circumstances surrounding the sin, so that one does not come to sin. This brings redemption and victory over the enslaving nation, since by this means one distances oneself completely from the sin.
records.targetHebrew: יָדוּעַ דְּתִיקּוּן הַמִּדּוֹת – לְהַעֲלוֹתָן לִמְקוֹרָן. וְאָז תִּיקּוּן גְּבוּרָה דִּקְלִפָּה – בִּגְבוּרָה דִּקְדוּשָּׁה, לְקַנֹּאות בְּעוֹבְרֵי רְצוֹנוֹ; וְתִיקּוּן תַּאֲוַת דִּקְלִפָּה – בְּתַאֲוָה דִּקְדוּשָּׁה, לְהִתְאַוּוֹת לַה'. וְאָמְנָם הַנִּצּוּחַ הוּא עַל יְדֵי הַהִיפּוּךְ; אֲבָל זֶה לְמִי שֶׁכְּבָר נִצַּח. וְכֵן כָּתַב בַּתַּנְיָא פֶּרֶק כז, שֶׁהוּא רַק לְצַדִּיק גָּמוּר, שֶׁכָּל הַמַּחֲשָׁבוֹת זָרוֹת הוּא רַק הַבָּאוֹת לוֹ מֵאֲחֵרִים, עַיֵּין שָׁם. וְהַיְינוּ, כִּי מִי שֶׁהוֹלֵךְ בַּמִּלְחָמָה, הוֹלֵךְ נֶגֶד חֲבֵירוֹ: וְאִם חֲבֵירוֹ מַבְעִיר אֵשׁ נֶגְדּוֹ, הוּא נוֹתֵן מַיִם וּמְכַבֶּה; אֲבָל מִי שֶׁכְּבָר נִצַּח וְהוּא שֶׁלּוֹ, כָּל הַדְּבָרִים שֶׁעָשָׂה הָאוֹיֵב נֶגְדּוֹ כְּדֵי לִלְחוֹם עִמּוֹ הוּא מְתַקְּנָם לְצָרְכּוֹ, שֶׁיִּהְיוּ מִשְׁתַּמְּשִׁים אוֹתוֹ תַּשְׁמִישׁ לְצָרְכּוֹ.
records.targetEnglish: It is known that the repair of character traits consists in raising them to their source. Then the repair of strength belonging to the shell is through strength in holiness: zeal against those who transgress His will. The repair of desire belonging to the shell is through desire in holiness: longing for God. Victory, however, comes through the opposite; this [use of the same powers for holiness] is for someone who has already won. So it is written in Tanya, chapter twenty-seven: it is only for a completely righteous person, whose foreign thoughts come to him solely from others; see there. Someone entering battle opposes his adversary: if the adversary lights a fire against him, he applies water and extinguishes it. But someone who has already won, and has taken possession, repairs for his own use everything the enemy made to fight against him, so that those same things serve his purposes.
records.explanation: Kometz HaMinchah distinguishes the stage of resistance from the later use of an opposing power for holiness. That distinction clarifies why the repentance described here requires safeguards even though it already brings a measure of redemption: Takanat HaShavin expressly says that the root of the past has not yet been completely repaired. The boundaries belong to the active struggle that prevents renewed sin, while a further transformation remains possible.

records.reverseExplanation: Takanat HaShavin gives a concrete form to the stage of resistance: one guards both against the sinful act and against the circumstances that lead toward it. Its distinction between genuine present repair and a root not yet fully repaired explains why meaningful progress does not by itself remove the need for boundaries.
records.reverseThemeTitle: Resistance precedes using a conquered power for holiness
records.reverseThemeSummary: Character repair ultimately raises a power to its source, but the struggle first requires opposing it. Only after conquest can the same power safely serve a holy purpose.

records.themeTitle: Repentance extends from stopping a sin to guarding its surroundings
records.themeSummary: Repentance can bring real release before the past has been completely repaired. Extending restraint to the conditions around a sin prevents renewed descent and gives the work of return greater strength.
records.originHebrew: אֲבָל גָּלוּת בָּבֶל הוּא גָּלוּת הָרִאשׁוֹנָה שֶׁהָיְתָה בִּשְׁבִיל הַחֵטְא, וּגְאֻלָּתוֹ הוּא גְּאֻלָּה הָרִאשׁוֹנָה שֶׁהָיְתָה עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה ״שֶׁמְּבִיאָה גְּאֻלָּה״; וְזֶה נֶגֶד מִדַּת הַנֶּצַח — הַיְינוּ נִיצּוּחַ — שֶׁכָּל גְּאֻלָּה הוּא נִיצּוּחַ הָאֻמָּה הַמְּשַׁעְבֶּדֶת, שֶׁכָּל כֹּחַ שֶׁעֲבוֹדָה לְיִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא מִצַּד הַחֵטְא שֶׁהוּא בְּפֹעַל וְעַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁמְּתַקֵּן מִכָּאן וּלְהַבָּא לְבַד, דְּנִתְבַּטֵּל מַעֲשֵׂה הַחֵטְא בְּפֹעַל אַף שֶׁלֹּא נִתְקַן הַשֹּׁרֶשׁ דִּלְמַפְרֵעַ — וַעֲדַיִין אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיַּחֲזֹר לְקִלְקוּלוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁהָיָה אָז שֶׁגָּלוּ שֵׁנִית — מִכָּל מָקוֹם מִצַּד כֹּחַ הַתְּשׁוּבָה בְּתִיקּוּן דִּלְהַבָּא , שֶׁנִּתְבָּאֵר [בְּסִימָן א] בַּהֲבָאַת רְפוּאָה, דְּהוּא גַּם כֵּן אַף שֶׁלֹּא נִתְקַן בְּהֶחְלֵט, הָכִי נָמֵי הֲבָאַת גְּאֻלָּה עַל דֶּרֶךְ זֶה כִּי אֵין השי"ת מַבִּיט בָּזֶה אֶלָּא עַל מַה שֶּׁהוּא אוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה; רַק צָרִיךְ לָזֶה תְּשׁוּבָה בְּתֹקֶף יוֹתֵר, שֶׁיּוֹעִיל לְנַצֵּחַ הָאֻמָּה שֶׁכְּבָר נִמְסְרוּ לְיָדָן בְּסִבַּת הַחֵטְא שֶׁזֶּהוּ עַל דֶּרֶךְ ״עֲבֵירָה גּוֹרֶרֶת עֲבֵירָה״ וְ״הַבָּא לְטַמֵּא פּוֹתְחִין [לוֹ]״, שֶׁהֲרֵי שִׁעְבּוּדָם גּוֹרֵם לַחֲטוֹא עוֹד יוֹתֵר וְאָמְרוּ [פְּסָחִים קיח:] דִּ״כְלוּם יֵשׁ עֶבֶד שֶׁרַבּוֹ נוֹתֵן לוֹ מַתָּנָה וְחוֹזֵר וְנוֹטְלָהּ מִמֶּנּוּ״; וְאַף דְּגָלוּת יִשְׂרָאֵל חָלִילָה לֹא הָיָה דֶּרֶךְ מַתָּנָה כְּלָל, מִכָּל מָקוֹם הֲרֵי לְפִי שָׁעָה נִגְזַר לִהְיוֹת תַּחַת יָדָם, וְצָרִיךְ עַל זֶה מִשְׁפָּט בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ שֶׁיּוּכְלוּ לְנַצְּחָם וְלָצֵאת מִתַּחַת יָדָם וְשֹׁרֶשׁ הַתְּשׁוּבָה, דְּהוּא הַחֲרָטָה מֵהַחֵטְא וּשְׁמִירָה מִמֶּנּוּ לְהַבָּא — הִנֵּה קַבָּלַת הַשְּׁמִירָה מִגּוּף הַחֵטְא עַצְמוֹ מֵבִיא רְפוּאָה לְמַכַּת הַחֵטְא, וְהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּתוֹ הוּא קַבָּלַת גְּדֵרִים וּסְיָיגִים עַל עֶצֶם הַדָּבָר שֶׁסְּבִיבוֹת הַחֵטְא, שֶׁלֹּא יָבוֹא לִידֵי חֵטְא — זֶהוּ הַגּוֹרֵם גְּאֻלָּה וְנִיצּוּחַ לָאֻמָּה הַמְשֻׁעְבֶּדֶת, בִּהְיוֹתוֹ מִתְרַחֵק עַל יְדֵי זֶה מֵהַחֵטְא לְגַמְרֵי
records.originEnglish: The Babylonian exile, however, was the first exile caused by sin, and its redemption was the first redemption through repentance, which “brings redemption.” This corresponds to the quality of netzach—that is, victory—for every redemption is a victory over the nation that enslaves, whose entire power to enslave Israel comes from sin in actual deed. Through repentance that repairs only from now onward, the sinful deed is annulled in practice even though its root has not been repaired retroactively. It remains possible that the person will return to his corruption, as happened then, when they were exiled again. Nevertheless, repentance’s power to repair the future, explained in section one concerning the bringing of healing even where the repair is not definitive, likewise brings redemption in this manner. For in this matter the blessed God looks only at what the person is at that time. Yet repentance of greater force is needed, so that it can overcome the nation into whose hands they were already delivered because of sin. This follows “one transgression draws another” and “one who comes to defile himself is given an opening,” since their subjugation causes still more sin. They said in Pesachim: “Does a master give a servant a gift and then take it back?” Although Israel’s exile was certainly not a gift, God forbid, they were nevertheless decreed for the time being to be under those nations’ power. A separate judgment is needed for them to overcome the nations and emerge from beneath their power. The root of repentance is regret for sin and guarding against it in the future. Accepting the duty to guard against the sinful act itself brings healing to the wound of sin. Its extension is accepting boundaries and safeguards concerning the circumstances surrounding the sin, so that one does not come to sin. This brings redemption and victory over the enslaving nation, since by this means one distances oneself completely from the sin.

records.targetHebrew: כְּתִיב (מִשְׁלֵי ח, טו): "בִּי מְלָכִים יִמְלֹכוּ", וְהִנֵּה כְּפִי הַפְּשָׁט הָיָה לִכְתּוֹב: "בִּי יִמְלֹכוּ מְלָכִים", אַךְ רָמַז בָּזֶה שֶׁאֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְמַנֶּה לְמֶלֶךְ רַק מִי שֶׁיּוּכַל לִמְלוֹךְ תְּחִלָּה עַל עַצְמוֹ, אוֹתוֹ מְמַנֶּה גַּם עַל אֲחֵרִים, כָּעִנְיָן שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק ד מִשְׁנָה א): "אֵיזֶהוּ גִבּוֹר? הַכּוֹבֵשׁ אֶת יִצְרוֹ". וְזֶהוּ "בִּי מְלָכִים יִמְלֹכוּ", הַיְינוּ מִי שֶׁמּוֹלֵךְ עַל עַצְמוֹ וְשִׂכְלוֹ מוֹשֵׁל עַל תַּאֲוָתוֹ, אָז "יִמְלֹכוּ", הַיְינוּ יִהְיֶה מֶלֶךְ עַל כֹּל, וְאֵין צָרִיךְ לְהַשְׁגִּיחַ עַל הַמִּתְנַגֵּד לוֹ, אַחֲרֵי שֶׁכָּל כַּוָּונָתוֹ לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם. וְזֶה שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וּמַלְכִּי צֶדֶק מֶלֶךְ שָׁלֵם", הַיְינוּ שֶׁהָיָה בַּתְּחִלָּה מֶלֶךְ צֶדֶק, שֶׁמָּלַךְ עַל עַצְמוֹ בְּצִדְקוֹ, וְאַחַר כָּךְ "מֶלֶךְ שָׁלֵם" – הוּא יְרוּשָׁלַיִם. וְזֶה הַטַּעַם שֶׁחוֹדֶשׁ נִיסָן הוּא רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה לַמְּלָכִים, וּמֵהָרָאוּי לִהְיוֹת בְּרֹאשׁ חוֹדֶשׁ סִיוָון כִּי בוֹ נִתְּנָה תוֹרָה לְיִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁכְּתִיב בָּהּ "בִּי מְלָכִים וְכוּלֵי"; אַךְ לַאֲשֶׁר שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר תְּחִלָּה "בִּי מְלָכִים" וְאַחַר כָּךְ "יִמְלֹכוּ", הַיְינוּ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה מֶלֶךְ עַל עַצְמוֹ, וְזֶהוּ בְּחוֹדֶשׁ נִיסָן שֶׁיִּשְׂרָאֵל מְצוּמְצָמִין בַּאֲכִילַת לֶחֶם עוֹנִי וּמְקַבֵּל עָלָיו עוֹל הַבּוֹרֵא יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְלֶאֱכוֹל מִיָּדוֹ פַּת יָבֵשׁ בְּלִי טַעַם וְלֹא מַעֲדַנִּים תַּחַת עוֹל בָּשָׂר וָדָם, כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת בְּמִצְרַיִם הָיָה לָהֶם רַב טוּב כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (שְׁמוֹת טז, ג): "בְּשִׁבְתֵּנוּ וְכוּלֵי", עַל יְדֵי זֶה "יִמְלֹכוּ", הַיְינוּ עַל כָּל הָעוֹלָם, וְזֶהוּ בְּחוֹדֶשׁ סִיוָון עַל יְדֵי שֶׁנִּתְּנָה בוֹ תּוֹרָה.
records.targetEnglish: It is written, “Through Me kings reign.” At the plain level it could have said, “Through Me there reign kings.” But this hints that the Holy One, blessed be He, appoints as king only someone who can first rule himself; that person He appoints over others as well. This accords with “Who is mighty? One who conquers his inclination.” Thus, “Through Me kings reign” means: someone who rules himself, whose intellect governs his desire, will then “reign”—he will be king over all. He need not attend to what opposes him, since his entire intention is for the sake of Heaven. This is “Melchizedek, king of Salem”: first he was a righteous king, ruling himself through his righteousness, and afterward “king of Salem,” which is Jerusalem. This is why Nisan is the new year for kings. It would have been fitting for it to be the first of Sivan, when Torah was given to Israel, of which it is written, “Through Me kings,” and so forth. But because it first says “Through Me kings” and afterward “reign,” one must first be king over oneself. This occurs in Nisan, when Israel restrict themselves to eating bread of poverty and accept the Creator’s yoke: eating dry bread without flavor from His hand, rather than delicacies beneath the yoke of flesh and blood. In Egypt they actually had much good, as it is written, “When we sat,” and so forth. Through this they “reign,” over the whole world. This occurs in Sivan through the Torah given then.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach makes inward self-rule a condition for the wider rule symbolized by kingship. His sequence from restrained eating in Nisan to Torah in Sivan gives an illuminating form to Takanat HaShavin’s movement from governing the conditions of sin to overcoming an external power. Both passages locate freedom in accepting divine service and ordering desire, with the wider victory growing from that inward work.

records.reverseExplanation: Takanat HaShavin explains how inward government becomes practical: guarding against sin expands into safeguards around the conditions that lead to it. This illuminates the preparatory restraint in Mei HaShiloach’s account of Nisan, while preserving the distinction between a real beginning of freedom and its complete realization.
records.reverseThemeTitle: Ruling oneself prepares for a wider freedom
records.reverseThemeSummary: Melchizedek’s kingship and the sequence of Nisan and Sivan express one order: a person first rules desire under God’s yoke, and only afterward receives the wider authority associated with Torah.

records.themeTitle: Redemption can begin within the place of exile
records.themeSummary: Zerubbabel’s birth in Babylon shows the exile already producing the beginning of release. The redeemer emerges from within the place whose power is to be overcome.
records.originHebrew: [ב] וּמַעֲלָה זוֹ הָרְבִיעִית, אַף שֶׁשְּׁלֵימוּתָהּ הוּא לֶעָתִיד כְּשֶׁיִּהְיֶה גְּאֻלָּה הַשְּׁלֵימָה עַל יְדֵי הַמָּשִׁיחַ מִזֶּרַע דָּוִד, שֶׁהוּא יְבָרֵר וִיגַלֶּה כָּל מַדְרֵגוֹת הַתְּשׁוּבָה כֻּלָּם עַל שְׁלֵימוּתָם הָרָאוּי — מִכָּל מָקוֹם כְּבָר הִתְחִילָה גִּילּוּי אוֹר מַעֲלָה זוֹ עַל יְדֵי זְרֻבָּבֶל בֶּן שְׁאַלְתִּיאֵל שֶׁהוּא מִזֶּרַע דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע"ה וְהוּא נְחֶמְיָה בֶּן חֲכַלְיָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא [סַנְהֶדְרִין לח.], וְנִקְרָא ״זְרֻבָּבֶל״ שֶׁנִּזְרַע בְּבָבֶל — וְהַיְינוּ לִהְיוֹת הוּא עִיקַּר הַגּוֹאֵל מִבָּבֶל וְהוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ עַל פָּסוּק ״שָׁם יִרְעֶה עֵגֶל״ עַל מָשִׁיחַ שֶׁגָּדֵל עִמָּם בַּמְּדִינָה, כְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע"ה בְּפָלָטִין מִצְרַיִם; דִּלְעוֹלָם הַגּוֹאֵל הוּא מִגְּדוֹלֵי מְדִינַת הַגָּלוּת דַּוְקָא, עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא [סַנְהֶדְרִין לט:] ״מִינֵּיהּ וּבֵיהּ אַבָּא נֵיזִיל בֵּיהּ נַרְגָּא״ וּזְרֻבָּבֶל שֶׁנִּזְרַע שָׁם, וְהַיְינוּ דְּעִיקַּר הַזְרָעָתוֹ הָיָה עַל יְדֵי מֶלֶךְ בָּבֶל עַצְמוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה] ״פַּיְּיסוּ לְגַדֶּלֶת, וְגָדַלְתָּ לְמַלְכָּה, וּמַלְכָּה לַמֶּלֶךְ״ דִּיכָנְיָה כְּבָר נִגְזַר עָלָיו ״כִּתְבוּ אֶת הָאִישׁ הַזֶּה עֲרִירִי״ וְגוֹ’, אֶלָּא שֶׁבְּבָבֶל גָּרְמָה לוֹ דְּהַגָּלוּת כִּיפֵּר כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [סַנְהֶדְרִין לז:] וְהַזְרָעָתוֹ הָיָה מוֹרֶה שֶׁכְּבָר פָּעַל גָּלוּת בָּבֶל פְּעֻלָּתוֹ, וּמִמֵּילָא מַתְחִיל מִמֶּנּוּ הַגְּאֻלָּה , בְּאֹוֽפֶן דְּשֵׁם זֶה מוֹרֶה עַל מַעֲלָתוֹ, שֶׁהַגְּאֻוֽלָּה נִצְמַח עַל יָדוֹ. וְרָאוּי הָיָה לִהְיוֹת אָז גְּאֻלָּה שְׁלֵימָה, אֶלָּא שֶׁגָּרַם הַחֵטְא כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּרָכוֹת ד.]
records.originEnglish: Although the perfection of this fourth level lies in the future, when complete redemption comes through the Messiah descended from David, who will clarify and reveal all the levels of repentance in their proper perfection, the light of this level already began to be revealed through Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, a descendant of King David. This is Nehemiah son of Hacaliah, as stated in Sanhedrin. He is called “Zerubbabel” because he was sown in Babylon: he was the principal redeemer from Babylon. This resembles what they said on “There the calf shall graze,” concerning the Messiah growing up with them in their country, just as Moses our teacher grew up in the palace of Egypt. The redeemer is always specifically one of the leading figures of the country of exile, in the manner of “From the forest itself comes the axe [that cuts it].” Zerubbabel was sown there: his very conception came about through the king of Babylon himself, as they said in Vayikra Rabbah, “They persuaded the governess, the governess persuaded the queen, and the queen persuaded the king.” For Jeconiah had already been sentenced, “Record this man as childless,” and so forth, but being in Babylon brought about [his having offspring], for the exile atoned, as they said in Sanhedrin. His conception showed that the Babylonian exile had already accomplished its work, and consequently redemption begins through him. His name therefore expresses his distinction: redemption grows through him. It would have been fitting for redemption then to be complete, but sin prevented it, as they said in Berakhot.
records.targetHebrew: אַךְ הָעִנְיָן עַל פִּי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַב בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ: "לֶךְ לְךָ – לְאַתְקָנָא גַּרְמָךְ, לְאַתְקָנָא דַּרְגָּא דִילָךְ וְכוּלֵי", וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ, שֶׁאַף שֶׁנּוֹלַד מִתֶּרַח שֶׁהָיָה עוֹבֵד עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, וּבְמָקוֹם שֶׁהָיוּ שְׁטוּפִין בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, לֹא יִפְחַד מִזֶּה, שֶׁאַדְּרַבָּה, מִזֶּה עַצְמוֹ יוּכַל לֵילֵךְ וּלְהַגִּיעַ לְמַדְרֵגָתוֹ. וְעַד דֻּגְמַת מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וּבִקַּשְׁתֶּם מִשָּׁם אֶת ה' אֱלֹהֶיךָ וּמָצָאתָ וְגוֹמֵר", וְהוּא אַחַר שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר "וֶהֱפִיץ ה' אֶתְכֶם בָּעַמִּים וְגוֹמֵר", אַל יֵרַךְ לְבַבְכֶם לְהִתְיָאֵשׁ פֶּן חַס וְשָׁלוֹם תִּתְקַלְקְלוּ לְגַמְרֵי, כִּי אַדְּרַבָּה, מִשָּׁם דַּיְיקָא "וּבִקַּשְׁתֶּם וְגוֹמֵר", שֶׁהַגָּלוּת יִגְרוֹם "כִּי תִדְרְשֶׁנּוּ בְּכָל לְבָבְךָ וּבְכָל נַפְשֶׁךָ", וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה "וּבִקַּשְׁתֶּם וּמָצָאתָ". וְכֵן אָמַר לוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ: "לֶךְ לְךָ" – לְאַתְקָנָא דַּרְגָּא דִילָךְ, מֵאַרְצְךָ וּמוֹלַדְתְּךָ שֶׁנּוֹלַדְתָּ בְּמָקוֹם גָּרוּעַ וְשָׁפֵל, וּמִבֵּית אָבִיךָ שֶׁהָיָה תֶּרַח עוֹבֵד עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה – מִזֶּה עַצְמוֹ תּוּכַל לְתַקֵּן דַּרְגָּא דִילָךְ.
records.targetEnglish: The matter follows what is written in the holy Zohar: “Go for yourself—to put yourself right, to put your own level right,” and so forth. God was telling him that, although he was born to Terah, an idolater, in a place immersed in idolatry, he should not fear this. On the contrary, from that very situation he could advance and reach his level. This resembles “From there you shall seek the Lord your God, and you shall find Him,” which follows “The Lord will scatter you among the peoples.” Do not lose heart and despair, fearing that, God forbid, you will become completely corrupted. On the contrary, precisely “from there you shall seek”: the exile will bring about “when you seek Him with all your heart and all your soul,” and thereby “you shall seek and find.” So too, the blessed God told our father Abraham: “Go for yourself”—to put your own level right—“from your land and your birthplace,” having been born in a degraded, lowly place, “and from your father’s house,” Terah having been an idolater. From that very situation you can put your level right.
records.explanation: Peri Tzadik states the inward form of the movement illustrated by Zerubbabel: “from there” means that distance and exile can themselves awaken wholehearted seeking. Takanat HaShavin supplies a historical pattern for that reading—the place of exile can bring forth the very person through whom release begins. Both passages preserve a real process of change; the Babylonian beginning is not confused with the complete redemption that sin delayed.

records.reverseExplanation: Takanat HaShavin gives a concrete historical illustration of the phrase “from there”: Zerubbabel is born in Babylon once exile has done its work, and redemption begins through him there. This deepens Peri Tzadik’s claim that the place of distance can participate in the growth of return rather than merely precede it.
records.reverseThemeTitle: Distance itself can awaken the movement of return
records.reverseThemeSummary: Abraham’s origins and Israel’s exile need not end in spiritual ruin. Precisely from those conditions, a person can be awakened to seek God with the whole heart.

records.themeTitle: Healing and redemption remove different obstacles to the heart’s will
records.themeSummary: The hidden will to serve God remains beneath the obstruction of the inclination and subjugation. Healing addresses the wound within the soul; redemption extends the repair into freedom from the external power.
records.originHebrew: [א] ״שֶׁמַּקְרֶבֶת״ אוֹ ״מְבִיאָה גְּאֻלָּה לְעוֹלָם״, וְזֶהוּ הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת מִדַּת ״מְבִיאָה רְפוּאָה״ דְּאֵלּוּ שְׁלֹשׁ הַקּוֹדְמוֹת מוֹלִידוֹת עוֹד שְׁלֹשׁ מַעֲלוֹת אֲחֵרוֹת, מִצַּד הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת וְהַמְשָׁכַת שֶׁפַע כְּמִדָּתוֹ יִתְבָּרֵךְ בְּכָל דָּבָר טוֹב; וְהַגְּאוּלָּה הוּא הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַתִּיקּוּן לְהַבָּא יוֹתֵר מֵרְפוּאָה וְהַיְינוּ דְּיָדוּעַ מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר [בְּרָכוֹת יז.] ״רְצוֹנֵנוּ לַעֲשׂוֹת רְצוֹנְךָ, וּמִי מְעַכֵּב? שְׂאוֹר שֶׁבָּעִיסָּה וְשִׁעְבּוּד מַלְכֻיּוֹת״ וְהַיְינוּ רָצוֹן הָאֲמִיתִּי הַנֶּעְלָם שֶׁבַּנֶּפֶשׁ הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִי, זֶרַע יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ ע"ה, אֵין לוֹ שַׁיָּיכוּת לְשׁוּם חֵטְא, שֶׁהֵם רַק כְּחוּצֵי הַסּוֹבְבִים לְאָסָא, מֵרְצוֹנוֹת זָרוּת הַנִּמְשָׁכוֹת לַלֵּב עַל יְדֵי יֵצֶר הָרַע וְאֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם וּרְפוּאָה הוּא לְחֹלִי שֶׁבַּנֶּפֶשׁ עַצְמוֹ, לְהִינָּצֵל מֵהַשְּׂאוֹר שֶׁבָּעִיסָּה עַצְמָהּ; וּגְאֻלָּה הוּא מִשִּׁעְבּוּד מַלְכוּיוֹת. וְזֶהוּ דַּרְגָּא דְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע"ה שֶׁהוּא הַגּוֹאֵל הָרִאשׁוֹן לְיִשְׂרָאֵל וּבְעֵת מַתַּן תּוֹרָה, שֶׁנִּתְקַן הַקּוֹדֵם, נַעֲשָׂה חֵרוּת לְגַמְרֵי מִמַּלְכֻיּוֹת וּמִיֵּצֶר הָרַע וְגַם מִמַּלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לֶעָתִיד אֲבָל זֶה הָיָה קֹדֶם שֶׁיֶּחֱטָא, דְּגָלוּת מִצְרַיִם לֹא הָיָה בִּשְׁבִיל חֵטְא — שֶׁהֲרֵי עֲדַיִין לֹא נִיתְּנָה תּוֹרָה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה חֵטְא — רַק הָיָה הֲכָנָה לְמַתַּן תּוֹרָה; וּלְאַחַר הַחֵטְא, שֶׁיְּעַיֵּל הַתְּשׁוּבָה לְהַחֲזִיר לְמַדְרֵגָה זוֹ, זֶה לֹא הָיָה עֲדַיִין כִּי הֲקָמַת עֻלָּה שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה הָיָה עַל יְדֵי דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע"ה, וּמִזַּרְעוֹ אַחֲרָיו הֵם הַמַּגְלִים וּמְעוֹרְרִים מַעֲלוֹת וּמַדְרֵגוֹת הַתְּשׁוּבָה אַחַת לְאַחַת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּתְבָּאֵר מִשְּׁלֹמֹה וְחִזְקִיָּה
records.originEnglish: “It brings redemption near,” or “it brings redemption to the world”: this is the extension of the quality of “bringing healing.” The three preceding qualities produce three further levels through the expansion and drawing down of bounty, in accordance with His way in every good matter. Redemption extends the repair of the future further than healing. The saying is known: “Our will is to do Your will. What prevents us? The leaven in the dough and subjugation to the kingdoms.” This means that the true, hidden will in the soul of an Israelite, a descendant of Jacob our father, has no connection with any sin. Sins are only like thorns surrounding a myrtle, foreign desires drawn into the heart through the evil inclination and the nations of the world. Healing concerns the sickness within the soul itself: being saved from the leaven in the dough itself. Redemption concerns subjugation to the kingdoms. This is the level of Moses our teacher, Israel’s first redeemer. At the giving of Torah, when what had gone before was repaired, there was complete freedom from the kingdoms, the evil inclination, and even the Angel of Death, as there will be in the future. But this was before sin. The Egyptian exile was not because of sin—for Torah had not yet been given for there to be sin—but was preparation for the giving of Torah. After sin, the ability of repentance to restore this level had not yet been realized. King David established the yoke of repentance; his descendants after him reveal and awaken its levels one by one, as was explained concerning Solomon and Hezekiah.

records.targetEnglish: Likewise, someone who is wicked in actual deed is so only through the inclination; it does not come from his heart. As written in Berakhot: “It is revealed and known that our will [is to do Your will; what prevents us? The leaven in the dough],” and so forth. This is also the well-known explanation of Maimonides in chapter two of the Laws of Divorce for “they compel him until he says, ‘I am willing.’” Although he sins in deed and is consequently called wicked, nevertheless “even the sinners of Israel are full of remorse.” A thought of regret in the heart suffices for someone to be called wholly righteous, as stated in Kiddushin. There is no Israelite sinner who does not regret for some moment after the pleasure has passed and the inclination is no longer inciting him, because of the depth of good within his heart. Therefore, “Even though he has sinned, he is Israel”: that depth of good cannot be severed from him.
records.explanation: Machshavot Charutz describes how the hidden good becomes recognizable: actual sin does not erase the depth of the heart, and remorse can emerge after the attraction has passed. This gives a psychological expression to Takanat HaShavin’s distinction between the true will and the obstacles surrounding it. Healing can therefore uncover a will that remains present, while the section’s further stage of redemption removes the external conditions that impede its expression.

records.themeTitle: Safeguards make the work of return concrete in a generation
records.themeSummary: Nehemiah translates repentance into renewed commitment and practical boundaries suited to the generation. Some safeguards answer a temporary need; their purpose is to keep the people from returning to the same failure.
records.originHebrew: [ד] וּנְחֶמְיָה הוּא הָיָה הָרִאשׁוֹן לְחַדֵּשׁ גְּזֵירוֹת וּסְיָיגוֹת חֲדָשׁוֹת בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, וּכְפִי הַנִּרְאֶה הָיָה הַמַּתְחִיל בָּזֶה, וְכַנִּזְכָּר בְּסִפְרוֹ קַבָּלַת אִיסּוּר מֻקְצֶה וּמַשָּׂא וּמַתָּן בְּשַׁבָּת וְכֵן אַחֲרָיו כָּל חֲבֵירָיו אַנְשֵׁי כְּנֶסֶת הַגְּדוֹלָה הֵם בַּעֲלֵי הַתַּקָּנוֹת וְהַסְּיָיגוֹת בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, וְהִזְהִירוּ עַל זֶה בְּפֵירוּשׁ בִּשְׁלוֹשָׁה דְּבָרִים שֶׁאָמְרוּ [פ"א דְּאָבוֹת] ״וַעֲשׂוּ סְיָיג לַתּוֹרָה״ וּמוֹסִיף עֲלֵיהֶם נְחֶמְיָה בַּעֲשִׂיַּית סְיָיג דִּלְצֹרֶךְ שָׁעָה, אַף שֶׁאֵינוֹ רָאוּי לְהִתְקַיֵּים לְעוֹלָם — שֶׁהֲרֵי בְּמֻקְצֶה הִתִּירוּ וְחָזְרוּ וְהִתִּירוּ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [שַׁבָּת קכג:] ״בִּימֵי נְחֶמְיָה בֶּן חֲכַלְיָה נִשְׁנֵית מִשְׁנָה זוֹ״ — וְהַכֹּל כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁרָאָה צֹרֶךְ לִגְדֹּר הַדּוֹר שֶׁלֹּא יָשׁוּבוּ לְכִסְלָה אַף הוּא חִידֵּשׁ עִנְיַן חֲזָרַת קַבָּלַת הַתּוֹרָה, שֶׁבָּאוּ עַל הֶחָתוּם בְּאָלָה וּשְׁבוּעָה לִשְׁמוֹר תּוֹרַת ה’ כַּכָּתוּב בְּסִפְרוֹ; וּמִבֵּית אֲבוֹתָיו לְמָדָהּ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע"ה ״נִשְׁבַּעְתִּי וָאֲקַיֵּמָה״ וְגוֹ’, וְלָמְדוּ מִזֶּה [נְדָרִים ח.] דְּנִשְׁבָּעִין לְקַיֵּים הַמִּצְוָה לְזָרוֹזֵי נַפְשֵׁיהּ וְאַף הוּא קִיבְּלָהּ מִזְּקֵנוֹ בֹּעַז שֶׁאָמַר ״חַי ה’ שִׁכְבִי [עַד הַבֹּקֶר]״, וְאָמְרוּ זַ"ל [סִפְרֵי] לְיִצְרוֹ נִשְׁבַּע; וּבָא נְחֶמְיָה וּפִירְסְמָהּ לְעֵצָה זוֹ בְּכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְכָל עִנְיָנָיו וּמַעֲשָׂיו הָיָה בְּעִנְיָן זֶה — לְהוֹסִיף גְּדֵרִים וְזֵירוּזִים אַלְּהַבָּא שֶׁלֹּא יַעַבְרוּ עוֹד — וְעִנְיָן זֶה דִּתְשׁוּבָה הוּא הַמֵּבִיא גְּאֻלָּה וְנִרְאֶה דְּדָרְשִׁינַן עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא [בִּמְגִילָּה טו:] עַל פָּסוּק ״וּלְרוּחַ מִשְׁפָּט״ — ״זֶה הַדָּן אֶת יִצְרוֹ״, וּפֵירֵשׁ רַשִׁ"י כּוֹפֵהוּ לָשׁוּב בִּתְשׁוּבָה וּמִתְגַּבֵּר עַל יִצְרוֹ; וְדָבָר זֶה דִּשְׁפִיטַת הַיֵּצֶר הוּא הַמְקָרֵב גְּאֻלָּה
records.originEnglish: Nehemiah was the first to introduce new decrees and safeguards in Israel; as it appears, he began this work. His book records the acceptance of the prohibition of muktzeh and of trade on Shabbat. After him, all his colleagues, the Men of the Great Assembly, were the authors of enactments and safeguards in Israel. They explicitly urged this in the three things they said: “Make a fence for Torah.” Nehemiah added the making of a safeguard for a temporary need, even where it was not suited to endure forever. Concerning muktzeh, they permitted and then permitted further, as they said: “This teaching was taught in the days of Nehemiah son of Hacaliah.” Everything followed what he saw the generation needed as a boundary, so that they would not return to folly. He also introduced a renewed acceptance of Torah: they signed under a curse and an oath to observe God’s Torah, as written in his book. He learned this from his ancestral house, as King David said, “I have sworn, and I shall fulfill,” and so forth; from this they learned that one may swear to fulfill a mitzvah in order to spur oneself on. David in turn received this from his ancestor Boaz, who said, “As the Lord lives, lie down [until morning].” The Sages said that he swore against his inclination. Nehemiah came and made this counsel known throughout Israel. All his concerns and actions lay in this work: adding boundaries and encouragement for the future so that they would no longer transgress. This aspect of repentance brings redemption. It appears that we expound this in the manner of the statement on “and for a spirit of judgment”: “This is one who judges his inclination.” Rashi explains that he compels it to return in repentance and overcomes his inclination. This judging of the inclination brings redemption near.
records.targetHebrew: והיה בהסתר, והיה מגדיר עצמו בגדרים שיראה מפורש החיבור שלו עם אורו ית'. וזה וישם דניאל אל לבו וגו' וזה היה דניאל קובע בישראל, שאפילו יהיה בגודל ההסתר ע"י שיהיו מגדירים עצמם בגדרים וסייגים, יראו החבור שיש להם עם אור השי"ת.
records.targetEnglish: [Daniel] was in concealment and set boundaries for himself so that he would see clearly his connection with His blessed light. This is “Daniel set it upon his heart,” and so forth. Daniel established this within Israel: even amid great concealment, by setting boundaries and safeguards for themselves, they would see the connection they have with the light of the blessed God.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains a positive purpose served by boundaries under concealment: they make a person’s connection with God perceptible in conduct. This illuminates Nehemiah’s practical program in Takanat HaShavin. Renewed commitment becomes particular acts of restraint that sustain the relationship during the work of return, while Rav Tzadok also retains the need to fit a safeguard to its generation and, where appropriate, to its temporary purpose.
